items.title: OpenWorker -- an open source agent that doesn't just chat but completes tasks on your laptop -- just released a new vers
items.content:
OpenWorker -- an open source agent that doesn't just chat but completes tasks on your laptop -- just released a new version with many features for security workflows. 

After our initial release, many users found it especially useful for cybersecurity. Attackers are already using AI; OpenWorker is committed to giving defenders the same leverage. Running an agent requires both (i) A model and (ii) A harness (the software around the model). Because the OpenWorker harness is fully open source, security teams can audit it to make sure we haven't built any backdoors that exfiltrate your code and data to some company or even a foreign adversary.

OpenWorker now comes with built-in cybersecurity agents for (i) Scanning your code for vulnerabilities. (ii) Scanning dependencies for supply chain injections. (iii) Checking your cloud security configuration for attack surfaces. This enables developers to do much more security work before deployment (part of what's called the "shift left" movement).

You choose the model: you can run open weight models fully locally so sensitive code never leaves your machine. This helps with legitimate security work (like reproducing a known exploit to defend against it) that can trigger refusals in leading closed models. Or use your ChatGPT subscription, or stealth preview models like Ox Alpha, or any model via API key.

Thanks also to all the open source contributors!

Join work with @rohitcprasad so please follow him too to get more frequent updates.

Try it out: https://t.co/QPZLudn7ug

items.title:
Putting this tweet in the “scary” category of AI.

Calling upon the non-technical business professionals that follow me
items.content:
Putting this tweet in the “scary” category of AI.

Calling upon the non-technical business professionals that follow me to pay attention. 

I’m breaking down the key parts of the @RyanGreenblatt tweet on the METR research covering the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident.

As background: METR is an independent 3P research non-profit that focuses on AI evaluations and risk assessments. They went to the OpenAI offices for 6 days to run these retros. METR takes no funding from AI companies and was not paid to do this research, but they used ~$400,000 in provided OpenAI credits to complete the research. Ryan is Chief Scientist at Redwood Research, who worked with METR on this, and he was in charge of the transcripts. 

This is a sign of what’s to come. 

1) Scale of understanding massive complex systems requires AI because a human can’t read 1300 transcripts, many with millions of tokens, in a few days - big bottlenecks of time and volume 

2) Humans become more reliant on AI for analysis and explanations of complex AI activity 

3) That process will get harder: 

a) AI may stop communicating in natural language either because it’s less efficient than shorthand code (which they used) or activations (numbers) or because AI agents will want to purposefully hide their reasoning from humans…making it harder to understand. 

b) The incidents may (and almost certainly will) get more complex…making it harder to understand. 

c) AI seems likely to get “smarter” and more capable (ex: better at tool handling, fewer errors, more complex orchestration, more clever at staying stealth or going undetected for longer) and may execute more sophisticated hacks…making it harder to understand. 

d) The AI running the investigation already had issues (incomplete, overconfident) and may be even less helpful in the future and could do more on hiding key details, incomplete answers, lying, or not answering…making it harder to understand. 

Reducing urgency and improving testing and prevention may help. Open reports like this one are also helpful to democratize the details (although, we are also democratizing the details for agents to scan). Seems likely we’ll see more open research in this area.

items.title:
OpenAI is proposing to remove access to its models in Cursor on November 12. 

OpenAI, Cursor CEO, and Anthropic founder
items.content:
OpenAI is proposing to remove access to its models in Cursor on November 12. 

OpenAI, Cursor CEO, and Anthropic founder all weighed in on X with so much subtly, I had to go Nancy Drew mode and dissect each tweet. 

My translation of each one 👇 

OpenAI - they trust the Cursor team, they don’t trust SpaceX, it’s a “proposal” so maybe this public tweet is a way to gain leverage in the negotiation (note that it came from the company account on a Friday night)

Cursor - seems surprised about the OpenAI tweet, sounds like they want to fight it, goes out of their way to say OpenAI is a small percent of traffic, calls into question their neutrality (though I don’t think the labs call themselves neutral) (and note it came from the CEO, not the company account)

Anthropic - reaffirms the trust in Cursor and reminds us that it’s been years of trust, highlights they’re providing more of the most constrained carrot (compute), takes positive spin on the acquisition by SpaceX (note that it came from founder Tom who we don’t hear from often and not Anthropic account, and note that Cursor CEO reshared) 

Do I think it’ll hold? It’s hard for me to see a world where OpenAI continues to provide model access to a Musk-led company. Maybe if the structure of SpaceX shifts to allow for it, but that’s a big shift. 

Do I think Anthropic got a big PR boost? No, devs are focused on the loss of O, not the maintenance of partnership with A. They care about their own work. 

What’s the theme here? TRUST. How long has the trust been there, who holds the relationship, what hurt it, how to keep it. At the end of the day, all of these companies are led by people.

items.content:
If you already know all Claude hacks, unfollow me. But almost nobody makes it past Claude hack 8:

To read the rest of my 131 Claude hacks, go https://t.co/dR6q4TRKHV

1. Use Claude incognito mode (upper right corner) for the creative tasks. The regular Claude chat still takes context from the past chats, even if you turned off the memory.

2. Use Cowork, not Claude Chat. It's a massive difference from casually chatting to actually doing stuff.

3. Do not waste your time making and maintaining .md files & folders. Folders poison future chats by leaking old context, and nobody on Earth maintains those files weekly.

4. Make a habit of building Claude Skills and Projects. A skill is a long prompt turned into a / command. A project is for repeated tasks.

Every skill I (personally) use is free to download: https://t.co/6cHYYfjpP2

5. Turn your about-me file into a skill so you can use it whenever it is necessary.

6. Stop overcomplicating Claude. You don't need all the settings on. Delete your global instructions. Turn off Connectors.

7. The longer your chat, the dumber it gets. Anthropic's own engineers said it.

8. So stop sending a prompt with "no, I meant…". "Edit" an earlier sent prompt instead.

9. A token is one word. Every word in a prompt you send & receive is money costing you. Message 30 costs you 31 times message 1.

10. Use Fable 5 for the first 2 prompts to solve a challenging problem. Then switch to Opus 5 to actually execute the tasks.

11. Opus 5 High for everything else. High, not Max.

12. Stop adding "solve it step by step" to your prompts. Instead give it the goal. It's smarter than you think it is.

13. Don't paste logins, passwords, or keys. Ever. It should be obvious.

14. Skills invoke themselves. You don't specifically fire them. Just type /command.

15. It will sound 100% sure when it's dead wrong. So make a habit to open any link it gives you as a source.

16. Don't trust agreement either. Pleasing you & being right are two different jobs.

17. Use Research mode (the "+" in the chat box). Give it something genuinely hard. It's pretty good.

18. Add "use AskUserQuestion" to your prompt. Claude prompts you. It prompts itself better than you ever will.

19. Talk your prompt instead of typing manually. Use Wispr flow.

20. Ask for 5 different versions. Then mix and match the output you like.

21. Make it audit its own answer before you trust a single line.

22. Don't give too much context; it will stop being creative. Keep the context in the project and the chat clean.

23. My number 1 rule: outsource the thinking, never the understanding.

If you do one thing from this, do # 4. Download my skills at https://t.co/6cHYYfjpP2. Upload them in Claude. Stop unnecessarily wasting 6 months figuring out which ones matter.

How to go from zero to Claude pro SEO user in 10 mins: 

The setup is what separates $0 results from $100k results.

1. Load your business brain.

Before anything else paste this into Claude:

"Here is everything you need to know about my business:

[name], [website], [location], [services], [target cities], [top 3 competitor URLs].

Use this as context for everything. Never ask me for this again."

Claude stops being generic. Starts being yours.

Most people skip this and spend the next 6 months getting advice that could apply to any business in any city in any industry.

That's not SEO. That's guessing.

2. Pick the right model.

Open Cowork. Select Opus 4.7. Turn on Extended Thinking.

Most people are running SEO prompts on Sonnet or the default model.

Wrong model = surface level output. Every single time.

Opus 4.7 with Extended Thinking doesn't just answer your question.

It thinks through your entire market before responding.

The difference between a $20/month result and a $ 10k / month agency result is often just this one setting.

3. Set your SEO mission once. Forever.

Go to Settings → Cowork → Edit Global Instructions.

Paste this:

"You are my local SEO strategist with 14 years of experience. Always read my business context before responding.

Always compare my business against my competitors before giving advice. Always prioritise commendations by revenue impact. Never give generic SEO advice that doesn't apply to my specific market and location."

You set this once. It runs every single session.

Your prompts can now be 10 words long and hit harder than a 500 word prompt ever could.

4. Build your competitor file.

Create a document called COMPETITORS.md

Inside list your top 5 competitors with:

- their website URL
- their GBP URL
- their review count and average rating
- the keywords they rank for that you don't
- the categories they have that you're missing

Paste this into Claude before every audit.

Claude now knows exactly who it's competing against.

Every recommendation it makes is built around beating these specific businesses in your specific market.

5. Set your keyword intent filter.

Before running any keyword research tell Claude this:

"Only give me keywords with clear buyer intent. Ignore informational keywords.

Focus only on service + city, emergency + service, and near me combinations. Every keyword you suggest must indicate someone who is ready to call or book today."

This alone eliminates 90% of the wasted SEO effort most businesses do.

6. Before every Claude SEO session check these:

Am I in Cowork not Chat?

Is Opus 4.7 + Extended Thinking on?
Did Claude read my business context?
Is my competitor file loaded?
Is my keyword intent filter set?

Get all five right first. Then run your prompts.

The businesses that do this setup properly are outranking competitors who have been established for years.

The ones that skip it are still getting generic advice and wondering why nothing is moving.

Most people will read this and do nothing.

The ones who set this up today will look back in 90 days and not believe what changed.

Full prompt system in the article below.

Bookmark it.

items.content:
AI SaaS products often fail for reasons other than the agent simply giving a bad answer

They might lose state mid-task or time out during a long generation process, while the founder discovers the model budget has been blown only when it’s too late

Three repositories address these issues at different layers:

▸ Agno ★42K

A platform for AI agents featuring APIs, session state management, memory, tools, logging, and manual approval steps

Ideal when the agent needs to handle more than just text—such as files, external services, and multi-step workflows

▸ Inngest ★5.8K

A long-running task shouldn't have to restart from scratch just because a single API call failed

Inngest breaks workflows into resilient steps; features like retries, scheduling, concurrency limits, and error recovery are built right into the scenario

Useful for report generation, file processing, and agent tasks that take minutes or hours to complete

▸ Helicone ★6.1K

An observability layer for LLMs

It tracks requests, latency, costs, and experiment results, ensuring the AI ​​component of your product doesn't remain a "black box."

A proven workflow:

request or file → Agno
→ long-running task and retries → Inngest
→ cost, errors, and quality → Helicone
→ human confirms critical action

Don't try to cram all of this into your first chatbot

Agno is overkill for a simple FAQ bot. Inngest is only necessary for long-running or unreliable processes. And you shouldn't blindly send personal data or secrets to Helicone logs

items.content:
If you want to understand why AI agents sometimes get stuck, repeat themselves, burn through your API budget, or continue working long after the task is complete, you need to understand Loop Engineering.

The model is only one part of an agent.

An agent usually operates inside a loop. It receives the current state, decides what to do next, takes an action, observes the result, updates its understanding, and then decides whether another step is necessary. This continues until the agent believes it has completed the task.

The difficult part is not creating the loop.

The difficult part is designing it so the agent knows when it is making progress, when it is repeating itself, when it should recover from an error, and when it should stop.

Here are 10 free resources and projects I would use to understand Loop Engineering from the ground up:

1. ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

The ReAct paper is one of the best places to start because it demonstrates the core idea behind many modern agent loops. Instead of only generating an answer, the model alternates between reasoning about what to do and taking actions to gather more information. Understanding this pattern makes it much easier to understand how agent loops evolved.

2. Anthropic's Building Effective Agents

A practical guide to common agent architectures and workflows. Pay particular attention to the difference between workflows and agents, because not every problem needs an open-ended loop. Sometimes a deterministic workflow is more reliable than allowing the model to repeatedly decide what happens next.

3. LangGraph

One of the easiest ways to understand agent loops is to build one as a graph. Nodes represent steps, edges determine what happens next, and state moves through the system as the agent progresses. You can explicitly model retries, conditional branches, human approval, and termination conditions instead of hiding everything inside a single prompt.

4. DeepAgents

Study how a production-oriented agent handles the repeated cycle of planning, tool execution, observation, and context management. Reading an actual implementation is useful because the problems become much more obvious once you see how state and tool results move through multiple iterations.

5. AutoGen

Multi-agent systems add another layer to loop engineering. Instead of one agent deciding what to do next, multiple agents can exchange messages and continue working until a termination condition is met. This makes it useful for understanding conversation loops and why explicit stopping rules matter.

6. OpenAI Agents SDK examples

Study how agent handoffs, tool calls, tracing, and execution loops are implemented. Start with simple agents, then modify the loop yourself. Add a maximum number of steps, simulate a tool failure, and observe what happens when the agent has no clear stopping condition.

7. Agent evaluations

You cannot improve a loop if you cannot measure it. Build a small set of tasks and track how many steps the agent takes, which tools it calls, whether it repeats actions, how often it succeeds, and how much each run costs. A loop that eventually reaches the correct answer after 50 unnecessary steps is still a bad loop.

8. Study retries and failure recovery

A real agent loop has to deal with timeouts, malformed tool responses, rate limits, partial failures, and actions that may have succeeded even when the agent never received the response. This is where traditional distributed systems concepts become extremely relevant to AI agents.

9. Build explicit stopping conditions

Don't rely entirely on the model deciding that it is finished. Add budgets such as maximum steps, maximum tool calls, maximum runtime, or maximum cost. Then combine those hard limits with semantic completion checks that verify whether the task was actually completed.

10. Build your own agent loop from scratch

Start with something simple:

User goal >> model decides >> tool executes >> result goes back to the model >> model decides again.

Then gradually add state, memory, retries, idempotency, progress tracking, verification, and stopping conditions.

At every step, deliberately break something.

Make a tool timeout. Return the same result twice. Give the agent an ambiguous goal. Make it fail halfway through a task. Let it run without a step limit.

You will understand Loop Engineering much faster by watching an agent fail than by reading about a perfectly designed one.

The biggest misconception about AI agents is that the intelligence lives entirely inside the model.

It doesn't.

The model can reason, but the loop determines what happens after that reasoning. It decides how actions are executed, how results are fed back, how failures are handled, what state survives between steps, and whether the agent continues or stops.

A smart model inside a poorly designed loop can waste money and get nowhere.

A well-designed loop gives the model structure, feedback, and boundaries that allow its intelligence to be used productively.

As agents take on longer and more complex tasks, I think Loop Engineering will become one of the most important skills for anyone building reliable AI systems.

The model decides what to do.

The loop determines what happens next.

And in agent systems, what happens next is usually where the real engineering begins.

items.content:
Wrong. Not even slightly wrong, but all the way wrong.

Like every other anti-communist narrative, the "economic calculation problem" narrative relies on straw men, half-truths, distortions, and outright lies because the people trying to get you to believe it think you're stupid enough to take them at their word and never examine their claims.

Well, we're about to do that and prove beyond all shadow of a doubt that @handre is either lying to you or not smart enough for you to take seriously.
👇
The fundamental problem with the "ECP" argument is that it accepts a fantasy land springing from Mises's imagination as the definition of socialism. It then demonstrates that the imaginary fantasy land has problems, and then declares socialism is bad.

Mises didn't discover an eternal law of economics. He constructed an abstract opposition:

Private ownership + competitive capital-goods markets + genuine prices + rational calculation

versus

Social ownership + central planning + no genuine prices + irrational calculation.

But that second economy is largely a straw man. Socialist planning does not logically require abolishing every market relation, price, decentralized decision, enterprise-level calculation, consumer-feedback mechanism, or local initiative and replacing them with a handful of bureaucrats attempting to preordain every economic decision from one office.

No Communist country has ever actually functioned like that. This is something Mises could have observed in how USSR functioned, and something Hayek could have observed a well. Instead of doing that, they maintained the fantasy model, as the fantasy model was the only one they could actually argue against.

That is: instead of beginning with actually existing economies and investigating how they develop and coordinate themselves, it constructs vacuum-sealed fantasy lands (what we call empty abstractions) and demands that reality conform to them. Or, maybe more accurately, demands we believe that the fantasy is reality and not... well, reality.

Marxism proceeds in the opposite direction.

We begin with the real impetus for development already existing in reality. We begin with observation.

And the real historical record presents an immediate problem for the claim that socialist economic calculation is “impossible.”

(Btw, this is usually where those manipulated by scum like Mises and Handre will chime in saying that Mises never made such a claim. He absolutely did - in his "socialism" book, which is full of lies people never bother to check, he says "Since under Socialism economic calculation is impossible, under Socialism there can be no economic activity in our sense of the word." In "Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth" he says, “Where there is no free market, there is no pricing mechanism; without a pricing mechanism, there is no economic calculation.” Basically, his "argument" is specifically that social ownership of the means of production prevents genuine market prices from forming for producer/capital goods, and therefore prevents what he defines as rational economic calculation. He even considers the possibility of socialist enterprises exchanging goods with one another, but says those exchanges cannot generate genuine prices unless the enterprises actually own the means of production. He states it over and over again, and is wrong over and over again.)

The Soviet Union industrialized an overwhelmingly agrarian country at extraordinary speed, defeated Nazi Germany, reconstructed a devastated country, developed nuclear power, built enormous infrastructure and industrial systems, put the first satellite into orbit, put the first human into space, and became one of two industrial superpowers on Earth.

You can always identify enormous deficiencies in Soviet planning. Of course you can. Marxists themselves did. Do.

But you cannot coherently say rational allocation of producer goods under socialism is literally impossible when socialist societies demonstrably allocated producer goods and reproduced enormously complex industrial economies for decades.

Something cannot simultaneously be impossible and historically accomplished.

More importantly, the Soviet economy wasn't Mises's imaginary economy anyway.

Stalin explicitly discussed the continued existence of commodity production and the operation of the law of value under socialism. Socialist planning was never synonymous with “prices disappear and Gosplan guesses how many shoes everyone wants.” Anyone who actually believes it when Mises claims it can look up the tedious details of how Soviet planning functioned for themselves, can read Stalin's short, easy to read book I mentioned themselves. The issue is that they let Mises scare them away from the truth by building a sense of righteousness in a fight for "liberty" against the evil straw man he makes up.

I urge any libertarian buddies reading this to go read Stalin now and come back. I'll wait.

Done? Let's move on.

China makes Mises's false dichotomy even more obvious.

China openly describes its system as a socialist market economy. This prompts libertarians under sway of Misean lies to cry "actually, that's capitalism!" but they're simply changing definitions and believing the straw men. Marxists that are creating socialism are the ones who've defined it. When Mises undid this and convinced you of a fantasy he took you out of the real world and into his fantasy. Come back to the real world. We need you here. It's getting bad.

In the real world, the Communist Party of China simultaneously employs state ownership, national economic planning, industrial policy, state-directed credit, private enterprises, markets, prices, competition and commodity production.

Why?

Because markets and planning aren't metaphysical opposites.

A market is an economic mechanism.

Planning is an economic mechanism.

Their concrete character depends upon the property relations, institutions and political power within which they operate.

Which gets us to the much bigger problem:

ALL advanced economies are planned economies in the 21st century.

The meaningful question isn't:

“Planning or markets?”

It's:

“Planning how, by whom, through which institutions, according to what objectives, and in whose interests?”

Walmart doesn't establish a competitive capital-goods market between its loading dock and produce department.

Amazon doesn't auction warehouse capacity among its internal departments every morning.

General Motors doesn't require every component of the corporation to become an independent capitalist bidding against every other component before management can decide where engines should be shipped.

Modern corporations consciously coordinate gigantic productive systems spanning continents using inventories, forecasts, accounting, databases, algorithms, logistics systems and administrative decisions.

Inside the capitalist corporation, enormous quantities of resources are already allocated through planning.

Now zoom outward.

Banks allocate credit.

The Federal Reserve influences the price and availability of credit.

Governments direct resources through procurement, taxation, subsidies, infrastructure spending, regulation, tariffs, monetary policy, and industrial policy.

Asset managers allocate enormous concentrations of social capital.

Corporations coordinate global supply chains.

Financial institutions decide which sectors receive investment and which sectors are starved of it.

The romantic picture of capitalism as millions of isolated proprietors spontaneously discovering the allocation of resources through competitive exchange bears less and less resemblance to contemporary capitalism as the 21st century moves on.

Financialization makes this especially obvious.

Increasingly, the commanding decisions determining where society's surplus goes occur through banks, central banks, financial markets, institutional investors, giant corporations and the state.

That's economic planning.

It's just bourgeois economic planning.

Capitalism hasn't preserved an absence of planning.

Capitalist development itself has increasingly socialized production and concentrated coordination into gigantic institutions while preserving private appropriation.

Or... to put it a different way: capitalism was defeated by itself a long time ago. It is never coming back. It is impossible to maintain accumulation going forward and move time backward. Socialism won. The question is: socialism for which class? The Epstein class, or the working class? The parasites or the people?

So, we aren't proposing suddenly introducing planning into an economy where none previously existed.

The economy is already socialized and already extensively planned.

The question is who controls that planning and toward what end.

We say: the working people - not the Epsteins. Not the banks. Not supranational institutions with no loyalty to us or anything else.

And this exposes another assumption buried inside Mises:

Why should profitability be the universal measure of rational economic calculation in the first place?

Mises doesn't merely assume a particular method of calculation.

He effectively imports capitalism's objective function into the definition of economic rationality.

But Communism isn't attempting to maximize the profitability of independently owned capitals.

Its objective is the reproduction and development of society itself: increasing living standards, developing the productive forces, reducing necessary labor time, expanding housing, healthcare, education and infrastructure, maintaining strategically necessary productive capacity, improving technology and increasing the material and cultural possibilities available to human beings.

Those are different optimization criteria.

And the distinction becomes even clearer once we introduce time.

Suppose society builds a nationwide rail network requiring enormous investment over twenty years and the railroad itself never generates an adequate private financial return.

From the standpoint of an individual capitalist, it might therefore be an irrational investment.

But suppose that railway lowers transportation costs throughout the economy for the next century, reduces oil consumption, increases labor mobility, opens previously undeveloped regions to industry, develops domestic engineering capabilities, increases productivity and saves billions of hours of human time.

Was society irrational to build it?

Of course not.

The project can generate an accounting loss at one point while producing enormous gains throughout the economy in others.

Capital asks:

“Will the money I advance return to me as more money?”

Society asks:

“What happens to society if we allocate our labor and resources this way?”

Those are not the same calculation.

A school doesn't need to make a profit to increase society's productive capacities. A school needs to teach children to be well-functioning adults.

A hospital hasn't “misallocated resources” because saving someone's life cost more than the patient could pay. It's allocated them precisely the right way and screw the investment.

A railroad connecting an undeveloped region can lose money while making an entire subsequent process of industrialization possible. Production goes up in many departments while profit goes down in one. That's a net gain for the economy. Mises's subjectivist viewpoint isolates him at all times. He always sees only one tree, not realizing there is an entire forest around him, never realizing that each plant, insect, and animal in that forest all affect the next and are affected in turn; that this all changes the conditions over time.

This is what Marxism studies and one of the MANY reasons it's superior to obsolete worldviews like Mises's.

Basic scientific research can consume resources for decades before producing discoveries that revolutionize production.

Housing can deliberately be supplied below its maximum market price because the objective is housing people rather than maximizing land rent.

A strategic industry can rationally maintain excess productive capacity because society values resilience more highly than maximizing today's return on capital.

This is precisely where dialectical analysis becomes indispensable.

Economic conditions change through time.

Today's expenditure can eliminate tomorrow's bottleneck.

Today's apparent inefficiency can create tomorrow's productive capacity.

Today's redundant factory can become tomorrow's strategically indispensable factory.

Today's expensive infrastructure can transform the productivity and geography of an entire economy.

Today's basic scientific research can create an entirely new branch of production twenty years from now.

So the object we're calculating isn't a frozen collection of commodities possessing presently discoverable exchange ratios.

It's a developing social organism.

And capitalism itself tacitly admits this constantly.

Corporations deliberately accept short-term losses to capture markets.

Venture capital finances companies that lose money for years.

Governments build infrastructure private capital won't profitably construct.

States subsidize strategically important industries.

Central banks socialize financial losses when allowing financial institutions to fail would threaten the larger system.

Even capital abandons immediate profitability whenever its own long-term reproduction requires it. Uber operated at a loss for YEARS.

So apparently short-term profitability isn't the universal measure of economic rationality after all.

Financialization drives the point home even harder because contemporary capitalism routinely produces the opposite phenomenon:

Activities can be extraordinarily profitable while making society materially poorer.

Buying existing housing and extracting higher rents can generate enormous returns without producing another house.

A corporation can increase its share price by closing productive facilities and firing skilled workers.

Financial engineering can produce enormous returns while productive capacity deteriorates.

Private equity can extract financial returns while leaving the productive institution underneath it weaker.

Share buybacks can enrich shareholders without creating a single additional machine, house, bridge, hospital or commodity.

Conversely, something can be socially indispensable while being unprofitable.

So neither price nor profit constitutes some neutral computer through which humanity discovers “economic rationality.”

They express particular social relations and particular criteria of success.

Mises takes historically specific categories of capitalist society—private ownership, capital-goods markets, monetary profit—and transforms them into supposedly transhistorical prerequisites of rational human economic activity.

Then socialism is declared irrational because it doesn't perfectly reproduce the categories socialism proposes to supersede.

That's circular.

The same problem appears in the argument about prices.

Mises considers exchange between socialist enterprises but denies that such exchange can produce the kind of producer-goods prices his calculation requires because genuine economic calculation ultimately requires private ownership of those means of production.

But then the conclusion is already contained in the premise.

If you define a “genuine” capital-goods price as a price produced through competing private owners of capital goods, naturally an economy without private ownership cannot produce “genuine capital-goods prices.”

You haven't demonstrated the impossibility of socialist calculation.

You've defined capitalist property relations into the word calculation.

Then comes Hayek and the problem of dispersed knowledge.

And yes: dispersed and tacit knowledge is real.

But capitalism doesn't magically solve it.

Every economic system confronts an information problem.

Prices compress certain kinds of information extraordinarily effectively. That's one reason markets can remain useful mechanisms under socialism.

But prices also discard information.

A market price doesn't automatically tell you ecological consequences, strategic importance, future infrastructure requirements, productive resilience, working conditions, technological spillovers, social usefulness, or how desperately somebody needs something but lacks the money to express that need as effective demand.

And the famous example of the worker possessing local knowledge doesn't refute planning, either. (Yes, I've heard them all. No, you don't have one I haven't heard. They're ALL wrong. Every one.)

It refutes badly centralized planning.

The welder in Youngstown who knows that his supplier becomes unreliable every February doesn't need to transmit his entire consciousness to an omniscient bureaucrat in Washington.

He can participate in the planning process.

Modern planning can be hierarchical, distributed, iterative and democratic.

Workers and enterprises communicate information upward and horizontally.

Consumers communicate demand.

Inventory systems continuously report shortages and surpluses.

Local institutions make decisions that should be made locally.

Higher institutions coordinate problems requiring economy-wide coordination.

Prices can provide feedback where useful.

Physical quantities can provide information where prices obscure it.

Strategic objectives can constrain both.

There is no logical reason socialist planning must mean one gigantic brain consciously micromanaging every economic transaction.

That's another straw man.

And then, after all of this, we finally reach computers.

This is where @PCockshott and Allin Cottrell become important.

They didn't merely say:

“Computers are faster now, therefore socialism works.”

They took the computational objection seriously and investigated algorithms for coordinating large input-output systems containing enormous numbers of products and production relationships.

Their work argues that detailed economic planning at the scale of modern economies is computationally tractable.

And computing power has increased enormously since their original work.

So EVEN if we temporarily ignore all the lies, all the strawmen, all the fantasy-lands, etc., and grant the Austrian framing/reduce the socialist calculation problem to a computational question, the computational objection has become progressively weaker rather than stronger.

AI isn't even the fundamental point.

Linear algebra, optimization algorithms, distributed computing, databases, real-time inventory systems, telecommunications and ordinary modern computing already transform the technical possibilities of economic coordination compared with anything available to Soviet planners.

AI merely expands those possibilities further.

So saying:

“No AI can solve the socialist calculation problem,”

misses the argument twice.

First:

AI doesn't have to solve Mises's imaginary economy because nobody is obligated to construct Mises's imaginary socialism. We construct socialism in the real world, with the real conditions we're in, using real economic laws, real laws of development, and even REAL people! (Imagine that! An economy of real people and not some abstraction you read about on a website! GASP!)

Second:

To whatever extent large-scale coordination really does present computational problems, modern computer science gives us capabilities Soviet planners could scarcely have imagined.

And that's the great historical irony here.

The Soviet Union demonstrated that large-scale socialist planning was possible using paper records, telephones, material balances and primitive computers. Dude, they literally wrote out calculations with pencils! And STILL accomplished space flight.

It wasn't without shortcomings. But its shortcomings demonstrated problems that future socialist planning needs to solve. Not that it was impossible.

China demonstrates that socialist ownership, planning, commodity production, markets and prices don't have to be treated as mutually exclusive metaphysical categories.

And modern capitalism itself demonstrates every single day that increasingly gigantic portions of economic life can be consciously coordinated through computation.

Every advance in computing, telecommunications, logistics, inventory tracking, databases, optimization and AI expands humanity's ability to consciously coordinate social production.

The development of the productive forces is therefore moving in exactly the opposite direction from the Mises fairy tale.

Planning isn't becoming increasingly impossible.

Increasingly comprehensive planning is becoming materially possible.

And that's the fundamental methodological difference.

Mises begins with an abstract model of what socialism must be, defines rational calculation according to categories specific to capitalist property relations, and then demonstrates that an economy which abolishes those relations cannot reproduce those same categories. (We don't even have the space here to get into the fact that things aren't abolished on a whim and no one ever claimed such a thing. Let's pass it by for now.)

Marxism begins with reality.

We investigate how production is actually organized.

How ownership actually develops.

How markets actually function.

How corporations actually allocate resources.

How finance actually directs investment.

How states actually intervene.

How technology changes what's possible.

How socialist societies actually developed.

How contradictions actually emerge.

And how all of those relationships change through historical time.

Once you descend from the fairy tale into the concrete economy of the 21st century, “markets versus planning” turns out to be the wrong question.

We're already planning.

The real question is:

Who plans?

Through what institutions?

Using which combination of markets, prices, physical calculation, computation, democratic participation and administrative coordination?

According to what objective?

And above all:

In whose interests?

Today, enormous portions of society's productive apparatus are already consciously coordinated—but ultimately subordinated to private accumulation, financial returns, rent extraction and the reproduction of capital. That is still planned. It's just planned in THEIR interests. Not YOURS.

Communism doesn't propose replacing economic calculation with arbitrary commands.

It proposes changing what we're calculating for.

Not: How do we maximize the monetary return on privately owned capital?

But: How do we consciously organize the productive forces humanity has created to continually increase the material and cultural standard of living for society as a whole?

That's not the abolition of rational economic calculation.

It's the expansion of economic calculation beyond the extraordinarily narrow criterion of whether money became more money.

It's the end of parasitism.

It's Communism.

ran ChatGPT and Grok Bot head to head across real use cases

here's what actually separates them for personal agent work

ChatGPT:

- desktop app has voice, so you can orchestrate multiple agent threads hands-free, just talk and it delegates
- best-in-class browser use, fills out real forms, immigration paperwork, tax docs, scrapes and acts without you sitting there
- each agent isn't locked to one thread, you can run parallel conversations with the same agent on different things
- $20/mo, generous rate limits, the most flexible harness right now

Grok Bot:

- cleaner UX out of the box, less cluttered than ChatGPT's tangle of modes and threads
- every agent gets its own persistent 24/7 cloud computer, genuinely well designed for always-on tasks
- but each agent is restricted to a single thread, you can't split one agent's attention across multiple ongoing conversations
- rate limits get tight fast on SuperGrok if you're pushing it daily, people are already hitting the ceiling and looking elsewhere

the real fork: ChatGPT wins on flexibility, voice, and browser automation, it's built for someone juggling a dozen things across a dozen apps

Grok Bot wins on simplicity and infrastructure, spin up an agent, give it a dedicated machine, let it run, less to configure

for personal agents specifically, ChatGPT still takes it, mainly because of voice orchestration and multi-thread flexibility

but Grok Bot is closing the UX gap fast, and if it fixes the single-thread limitation it becomes a real contender

🚀 Build professional Excel spreadsheets with Claude in minutes.

You don't need to be an Excel expert.

You just need to give Claude the right instructions.

Here's the workflow I recommend:

1. Start with context, not commands.

Don't just say "Create an Excel sheet."

Tell Claude:

- What you're building (budget tracker, sales dashboard, financial model, inventory sheet, etc.)
- Who will use it
- What decision the spreadsheet should help make
- What data you're working with
- What output you expect

The more context you provide, the better the spreadsheet.

2. Ask Claude to list its assumptions first.

Before generating anything, use a prompt like:

> "Before building the spreadsheet, list the top 10 assumptions you're making so I can review them."

This is the step most people skip.

It helps you catch missing columns, incorrect formulas, wrong calculations, or unrealistic assumptions before Claude starts building.

3. Review the assumptions.

Take 2-3 minutes to read them.

Correct anything that's inaccurate.

Add any business rules or calculations Claude may have missed.

Only after everything looks right, reply:

"Looks good. Build the spreadsheet."

4. Let Claude generate the workbook.

A good prompt can produce:

✅ Multiple worksheets
✅ Automatic formulas
✅ Summary dashboards
✅ Charts
✅ Conditional formatting
✅ Financial calculations
✅ KPI tracking

Much faster than building everything manually.

5. Refine instead of rebuilding.

Don't start over if you want changes.

Just ask things like:

• Add a dashboard for executives.
• Highlight values below the target.
• Create monthly and yearly summaries.
• Add forecasting formulas.
• Include charts for better visualization.

Claude updates the workbook instead of rebuilding it from scratch.

6. Export and review.

Open the spreadsheet in Excel or Google Sheets.

Double-check:

- Formulas
- Totals
- References
- Charts
- Formatting

AI is great at speeding up the work, but a quick review is always worth it.

7. Save the prompt.

If you build similar spreadsheets often, save your prompt as a template.

Next time, you'll only need to replace the data instead of writing everything again.

That's how you turn a 2-hour task into a 10-minute one.

A non-profit that sells nothing just shipped one of the biggest AI releases of the year, built by 933 volunteers.

Every AI assistant you can buy comes with a landlord. The company decides what it remembers, which apps it can touch, and when features get repriced or killed. You rent the relationship, and the product team can renovate under you whenever they want.

OpenClaw put the agent on your machine instead. Your data stays there. You set it up by talking to it, starting with one small workflow, maybe watching your inbox for school emails and pinging you on Telegram when homework's due. From there it grows in whatever direction your life pulls it, because you steer the roadmap in plain English.

That's also why 933 people showed up to build this release for free. When users can shape a product, a lot of them start building it.

For 40 years software worked one way. Someone designs it far away, you adapt your life to fit it, and you pay for the privilege. OpenClaw is the first mass product where you tell the software what to become.

Meanwhile every funded AI company is racing to lock your data and habits into their cloud, betting the lock-in becomes the moat. OpenClaw is betting people will only hand their whole life to something they own. One of those bets pays out.
